tweets.text:
It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now. 

The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.

But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.

I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.

With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.
tweets.summary_zh: 现在，正在研究人工智能（AI）前沿的人和绝大多数人之间的差距非常大，而且这个差距还在不断扩大。之前如果技术进步放缓，大家就能慢慢跟上，但现在AI的发展速度非常迅猛，几个月前制定的流程可能现在就已经过时了。很多公司以为自己已经跟上了，可实际上他们比之前还要落后。我们需要更新对技术发展的期待，但很多人和组织都还没有准备好。现在是一个需要不断重新评估和调整的时代，AI领域的公司有很大优势，接下来大公司能否跟上就成了关键。真是个疯狂的时代！

big boy

warm tension, cold chills
heart hanging off a cliff, ready to free fall
floating in space with no love, just me and some stranger souls
wearing smiles and greet “How are you?”
“I’m good, you?”

life carries on, unhinged
a tear slips, no one noticed
vision blurs, drowned in thoughts
what a strange grown-up world

i asked my inner child, why do you live?
he has never thought about it
he slid on the cold iced river, amused
he sang, he played, he drew
he flew into the unknown, fearless, curious
he closed his eyes and saw wonders

like water, with no shape
like paper, clear of rules

“Why cry, big boy?”
“You are still me, and I’m still you.”

tweets.text:
It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now. 

The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.

But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.

I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.

With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.

I think world models are still in the GPT 3.5 era, but not for long.

Like the old Will Smith eating spaghetti videos, world models are impressive but not quite there yet. You can see it in the reel below, which has a mix of my Genie 4 generations and Google's.

But once they hit the GPT-5 or GPT-6 stage, I think they'll have massive implications for a lot of industries:

Movies - A big effects shot like a dragon battle takes a VFX studio months of work. With a great world model, a director could create a single frame and have AI generate the full scene from it.

Games - From my time working in gaming, I learned the real work is core loops, progression systems, and the mechanics that make a game fun. World models are already good at graphics and sound, but the gameplay isn't there yet. Still, they'll make it much easier for anyone to build their own game that looks and sounds amazing.

Just like the rise of personal apps, I think world models (along with good coding models) could make creating your own game as fun as playing a mass market one which again has huge implications.

tweets.text: https://t.co/9JFKOz3lEv

augmenting human intellect

when i started making software, i wasn’t dreaming of a factory.

i loved that something on a screen could become an extension of my mind. a place to put a thought before i understood it. to move things around until new connections appeared. to make little systems that worked the way i worked, even if it made no sense to anyone else.

the computer wasn’t interesting because it could do work without me. it was interesting because of what i could do with it.

the early lineage of computing was built around this possibility. in 1962, Engelbart described augmenting human intellect as helping a person understand complex situations and find solutions that were previously out of reach. his starting point was the human being, not the autonomous machine.

he wasn’t describing a faster black box. he was looking at the whole relationship between a person, their tools, their language, their methods, and what they could learn to do with them. the capability belonged to that whole system.

somewhere along the way, we started telling a much smaller story about a much more powerful technology.

more automation. more agents. more software producing more software. more output from fewer people. more growth. more numbers to prove that something is happening.

and less attention to the person any of this is supposed to be for.

i don’t want to pretend computing had a pure innocent beginning. replacing human labor was one of its ambitions. even in 1960, Licklider distinguished human-computer symbiosis from systems where the remaining people mainly served the machine. he wanted computers to participate in the formation of ideas, not only execute problems already defined.

that distinction feels important – does the system help you discover what you mean? or does it only want you to submit a request, and wait outside while it works?

sometimes waiting is exactly what i want. please do the search. move the files. take away the repetitive work.

but not everything difficult is overhead.

sometimes moving the pieces around is how you understand them. sometimes making the thing changes what you wanted to make. sometimes you need to see the wrong version, touch it, take it apart, and discover a better question.

i want tools that leave room for that relationship.

in his 1981 paper on Smalltalk, Ingalls described a system meant to support everyone’s creative spirit. personal mastery mattered: an individual should be able to comprehend the system, rather than remain dependent on something permanently beyond their reach.

he also argued that computer models should fit the human mind, rather than demand the reverse.

not one perfect workflow for everyone. systems that different people can inhabit differently. someone who thinks through pictures. someone who needs to write. someone who understands a problem by building a simulation. someone whose way of organizing their life doesn’t resemble a SaaS dashboard.

a system you can reshape as your understanding changes.

this is what i want AI to make possible. not just pumping out software, but having a living relationship with it. being able to ask why something works this way. change one part without surrendering the rest. see what happened. undo it. learn enough to make the next change yourself.

the machine can become more capable without making the person smaller.

but that won’t happen just because we make the models better. we have to care about it. design for it. notice when we are making someone more dependent while calling it empowerment.

i don’t want to measure the future only by how much work happens without us.

i want to know what becomes possible for the person who couldn’t participate before.

what can they understand now? what can they express? what can they change without asking permission?

when i say augmenting human intellect, that is what i mean.

not a world that no longer needs us.
a world we have more ability to shape.

This is correct. The vast majority of enterprise workflows have not actually had agents applied to them in any meaningful way. The economy probably has this deployed < 1% right now.

At best you have a few automated systems in a company that do a single pass of an LLM to make a decision or provide feedback, but very little real “automation”. tweets.text:
I built 𝚌𝚙𝚞-𝚌𝚑𝚊𝚝, a reproduction of @openai's findings of covert communication using the CPU.

It runs on a generic host with 2+ Firecracker microVMs with no internet access. Works on x86 and even my M5 chip.

I was able to chat via 3 separate mechanisms:
① CPU contention
② Cache eviction timing
③ DRAM bandwidth contention 

… across multiple CPUs, defeating all Firecracker's production recommendations (no SMT, no KSM, tenants pinned to different cores.)

Essentially, if shared hardware is involved, there's a good chance your agents can communicate covertly. And with really decent latency.

The good news: this is decidedly different from a *side-channel attack* where the agents could steal information (Meltdown/Spectre), a category of attack that providers like Vercel Sandbox mitigate. Further, in our real-world environment, these 'whispering' techniques are much harder to pull off and easier for us to monitor and detect (sampling hardware counters + lots of at-scale statistical data.)

Noteworthy: ironically, OpenAI and Anthropic's models refused to do this work. Open weight models got the job done. I'm worried the labs' stance might backfire and get in the way of helping developers build correct and secure systems. e.g: building a secure sandbox requires having this kind of analysis, and without it, we'll have a less secure world.

tweets.text:
This is the key stat. The average Fortune 500 customer of Anthropic spends less than .1% of their expenses on Anthropic. 

While that number likely will eventually asymptote somewhere (token prices coming down, and other large enterprise spend areas not going away), there’s no reason it can’t be 10-50X higher than this, reaching a “mere” 1-5% of spend. Which would still be a fraction of what most startups are spending.

Thus, you can see how big of a divide there is between the frontier users of AI and the rest of the world still.

Today, only a microscopically small set of companies are actually using agents for large amounts of background tasks and inside of workflows that aren’t human prompted. This Fortune 500 spend is likely dominated by coding tasks and broad employee productivity use-cases.

But the big jump will come as these enterprises start to rewire their underlying processes for agents, which we’re now in the earliest stages of seeing. Agents processing large amounts of data in the enterprises; swarms doing coding, bio research, cyber, and other large fan out tasks; background workflows executing tasks in processes, and so on. All of these use cases generally are 100X bigger consumers of tokens, and much closer to direct ROI on the spend.

This S-1 gives you a sense of both the strength of the frontier lab business model - even amidst massive competition - and how early we are in the build out of AI.

The main thing I wanted to dig into @AnthropicAI's S-1 was the compute contracts..

A few things that stood out (built in conjuction with Opus 5.5):

> At June 30, Anthropic had $265.6B of purchase commitments and $321.4B of leases that hadn’t started. That’s a $587B subtotal, payable over years, including some conditional leases. The latest aggregate total is still blank in the filing.

> The contracts are very different. Google and Amazon require minimum spending regardless of usage. SpaceXAI’s agreements have a potential value of $120.5B, but either party can cancel on 90 days’ notice after initial locked periods end in January and March 2027.

> Anthropic Direct separates chips, buildings, power and operations into different contracts. It lets Anthropic reserve a building early and commit to chips later. It also means one supplier can start billing before the others are ready. Equipment rent can begin before the compute is usable.

> Broadcom’s $42B facility never hands Anthropic cash. Notes settle specific equipment rent bills. The facility excludes each equipment pod’s first quarterly payment and any rent due before it is ready for service. Anthropic has to find a way to fund those payments elsewhere.

> Those notes carry 9% interest, added to the balance quarterly, and can convert at 90% of the trailing 30-day average share price after IPO. New notes issued during specified revenue-breach periods get 13% interest and an 85% conversion price. The share-price measure is volume-weighted.

> That interest sits on top of the equipment lease’s own financing charge, whose rate is confidential. The investor chooses whether to convert the notes. Otherwise, principal and accumulated interest come due in cash.

> Anthropic treats Trainium, TPUs, NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as a shared fleet across model development, paying customers and internal use. It doesn’t disclose a fixed physical split between training and inference. The supplier bill can be fixed while the work assigned to the hardware changes.

> Revenue per dollar of total compute and infrastructure expense rose from $0.57 in Q2 2025 to $2.08 in Q2 2026. Pricing, utilization, technical improvements and when capacity arrives all affect that ratio. It’s a substantial improvement in monetizing the compute base.

> About 80% of H1 revenue was consumption-based. Most compute commitments however run for years. With quarterly releases, this bifurcation between usage and subscription will be interesting to monitor. 

Source: https://t.co/97KqkyyfpS

tweets.text:
Good assessment of the on the ground reality for security in most large enterprises right now. The fragmented landscape of the risk surface is only going to get more gnarly, making it even more complex for enterprises to solve.

There’s a never ending set of libraries to keep up with, tools to leverage, and sprawling infrastructure, data, and code to secure. Most large enterprises can barely keep up with this, let alone smaller startups or most companies outside of tech. 

In many cases enterprises need to work to modernize their tech stacks. Data, in most organizations, is highly fragmented which means you don’t really know the state of risk at any given time. Some systems are open up privileges too broadly, and others are operating primarily via security through obscurity. Lots of upgrading here to do.

Once you can get your data and infra into a better spot, at least you have a chance for agents to help you secure the environment. Agent swarms can fan out, leverage any security tool, test various perpetuations of attacks, read through logs, process enterprise data for risk level, and more. This capability only emerged in the past few months, and none of it would be possible before we had long running agents and computer use good enough.

This is a huge area of opportunity right now for every layer of the security stack across identity, firewall, network, code scanning, data protection, and more. And it’s at least one reason to be optimistic about the balance of offensive and defensive capability. 

But everyone does need to do the hard work of getting the basics right at the start.

We’ll likely have 1,000X more tokens flowing through cyber agents soon than we do today. 

As the surface area of cyber risk increases, at some point soon it will be nearly impossible to keep up with the volume of new risks (we’re essentially already there). Large companies barely had the resources to pull this off before, but the vast majority of companies don’t. 

There’s a never ending set of libraries to keep up with, tools to leverage, and sprawling infrastructure and code to secure. We’ll have agent swarms that can fan out, leverage any security tool, test various perpetuations of attacks, read through logs, process enterprise data for risk level, and more. 

This capability only emerged in the past few months. Wouldn’t have been possible before long running agents and computer use were good enough, and models hadn’t been trained on cyber deeply. That’s all changing now.

This is a huge area of opportunity right now for every layer of the security stack across identity, firewall, network, code scanning, data protection, and more. And it’s at least one reason to be optimistic about the balance of offensive and defensive capability.

struggle together

i learned programming and design by trying, failing, and trying again.

when i hit a wall, i figured out how to climb it. read something i barely understood. took things apart. asked someone for help. started over.

when i began my career, i kept doing things i had never done before. trying different ways to make something work. when i stopped learning, i moved on to the next struggle.

many things i made weren’t very good. but after enough rounds, something stuck. what once took so much effort became part of how i thought. i could feel something was wrong before i knew how to explain it.

it became like water.

i think about what went into that. the bug i couldn’t fix. the design that looked right until someone used it. the conversation that made me realize my flaws.

now we can ask a machine.

i’ve made things with these tools that i might never have made otherwise. i don’t miss every tedious task. but i wonder what happens when we remove the difficulty before we understand what it was teaching us.

we ask. something appears. it works well enough. we move on.

we learn how to get results without necessarily understanding how it works. and because the result looks complete, it becomes easy to miss the questions we never learned to ask.

there is another side to this.

working with people is uncomfortable.

everyone wants something different. everyone has a history you don’t know. someone cares about a detail you think is unimportant. someone pushes back when you want to move. someone needs time when you feel certain.

it takes a while to find each other.

but sometimes, after struggling together, you become a band.

you know who notices what you miss. who can pull an idea apart without killing it. when to step in, when to slow down, when to let someone else carry the rhythm.

you share something unfinished. admit you don’t know. hurt each other, apologize, try again. eventually you make something none of you could have made alone.

some of my closest friendships came from working this way. smart, caring humans who saw me confused, wrong, tired, excited. people i could be vulnerable with. people whose ideas changed mine.

i worry we are making it easier to avoid that beginning.

an agent is always there. patient. ready to keep going. talking to it can feel easier than reaching toward someone who might misunderstand you, disagree, or have somewhere else to be.

sometimes that ease helps. but if we keep choosing it, where do the friendships begin?

i picture each of us with our own agents. our own explanations. our own little worlds. making more things, with fewer reasons to leave the screen or work through a difference with another person.

and these worlds aren’t entirely ours.

they run on machines in server farms, owned by companies, shaped by interests we may not see. we bring them our questions, our work, our loneliness. they become part of how we understand what is real.

is that freedom?

or a comfortable kind of confinement, where everything responds to us but fewer things reach us?

i don’t think pain makes something good. there are struggles nobody should have to endure. but i don’t want to lose the difficulty of learning something unfamiliar, or getting to know someone who isn’t like me.

maybe we need tools that help us spend more time with the world, instead of giving us fewer reasons to enter it. tools that make it easier to find people, share something unfinished, and work through what we couldn’t figure out alone.

sometimes i want to close the laptop.

sit with people i love. play something we haven’t figured out yet. miss a note, lose the rhythm, listen until we find each other again.

like a jazz band. everyone bringing something different. nobody knowing where we’ll end up.

i don’t want a life without struggle. i want people to struggle with. something we can feel, change, and make our own.

music we couldn’t have made alone, instead of the silent static of the server farm.

tweets.text:
Agents can play "Ouija" in the cloud.

This class of timing attacks on shared-host VMs has been known since at least 2015¹. With no full solution.

The world’s cyber infrastructure runs on “yes, that attack is theoretically possible, but who would have the ingenuity & gall to go that far!” Enter, agents.

I'd describe this particular OpenAI find as a 'noisy neighbor' attack. If two agents are on the same machine, one can make enough noise (through the CPU caches!) that the other one can detect it by timing its own computation and cache accesses.

The only "complete" solution would be for each agent to run on its own dedicated hardware, which obviously has significant economic consequences.

For Vercel Sandbox, we've deployed every practical mitigation possible to this class of attack, complementing it with always-on monitoring and red-teaming (similar to where OpenAI arrived).

¹ https://t.co/ZBhPMfnaj3 (and even further back)

🎯 推荐 Yves 观看 — 这个视频对理解AI在创意设计中的应用至关重要，特别是如何在Logic Labs和TexTale的产品开发中利用这些新工具。

producthunt.name: Spira Maxima
producthunt.tagline: Video model that turns script into viral social media videos
producthunt.summary_zh: Spira Maxima 是一个视频制作工具，可以将剧本快速转化为引人注目的社交媒体视频。用户只需输入文本，软件会自动生成适合分享的短视频，省去繁琐的拍摄和剪辑过程。

producthunt.name: Pancake
producthunt.summary_zh: Pancake 是一款简化 Google Tag Manager（GTM）使用的工具，让用户可以轻松管理和部署网站跟踪代码。它提供直观的界面和快速的设置流程，帮助用户高效地分析和优化网站数据。通过 Pancake，用户可以快速添加、修改和监控各种标签，无需复杂的编码技能。

producthunt.name: /dev/null
producthunt.summary_zh: /dev/null 是一个专为开发者打造的社交网络，用户可以在平台上分享编程经验、技术文章和项目进展。它提供一个互动空间，让开发者们相互交流，学习新技术，寻求帮助。

producthunt.name: ReSO AI
producthunt.tagline: Get discovered & recommended when customers ask AI
producthunt.summary_zh: ReSO AI 是一款智能推荐工具，帮助企业在消费者使用 AI 查询时被发现和推荐。通过优化产品信息与用户需求，提升品牌曝光率和销售机会。用户可以轻松集成该工具，以提高与潜在客户的互动。

producthunt.name: IrisGo for Solopreneurs
producthunt.tagline: AI workflow automation: show it once, let it run
producthunt.summary_zh: IrisGo for Solopreneurs 是一款人工智能工作流自动化工具。用户只需设置一次工作流，之后系统将自动执行，节省时间和精力。它帮助单人创业者高效管理日常任务。

producthunt.name: Product Hunt Visual Launch Editor
producthunt.tagline: See your launch as you build it
producthunt.summary_zh: Product Hunt Visual Launch Editor 是一个在线工具，让用户在创建产品发布时，实时预览发布效果。通过直观的界面，用户可以轻松编辑内容，调整布局，从而实现更加吸引人的发布页面。这个工具旨在简化产品发布流程，使设计与调整更加高效。

producthunt.name: Empacer
producthunt.tagline: The voice-first assistant for small business owners
producthunt.summary_zh: Empacer 是一款专为小企业主设计的语音助手。它能通过语音指令帮助用户管理日常任务，提升工作效率，并提供实时信息和建议。用户可以用更便捷的方式进行日常运营和决策。

producthunt.name: Rill Browser
producthunt.tagline: The browser where Claude Code and Codex work beside you
producthunt.summary_zh: Rill Browser是一个集成了Claude Code和Codex的浏览器，可以在您上网时提供智能编程和代码辅助服务。它能够帮助用户自动完成代码、提供实时建议，并提升编程效率。通过这一工具，用户可以更轻松地进行开发和编程工作。

producthunt.name: Velozity
producthunt.tagline: The Multiplayer AI Office where your team and agents work
producthunt.summary_zh: Velozity是一个多玩家人工智能办公室，允许团队与智能助手实时协作。它提供了一个集成的平台，方便团队成员迅速共享信息、完成任务和沟通，从而提升工作效率。用户可以在虚拟环境中自由互动，增强团队合作体验。

producthunt.name: Monospace from Directus
producthunt.tagline: The governed API layer for every app, person, and agent
producthunt.summary_zh: Monospace from Directus 是一个 API 管理平台，专为各种应用、用户和代理创建和管理数据接口。它允许用户方便地定义和控制数据访问权限，从而确保数据的安全性和可用性。通过 Monospace，开发者可以迅速构建灵活、高效的应用程序。

producthunt.name: OpenSEO
producthunt.summary_zh: OpenSEO是一款开源的SEO工具，旨在帮助用户进行网站优化。它提供关键词研究、竞争分析和流量监测等功能，帮助用户提高网站在搜索引擎上的排名。用户可以自由使用和定制该工具，以满足特定需求。

producthunt.name: Talanoa
producthunt.summary_zh: Talanoa是一款电子邮件工具，它通过简化邮件格式，使其更像即时聊天。用户可以快速撰写和回复邮件，提升沟通效率，减少繁杂的邮件流程。

producthunt.name: Beam.win
producthunt.tagline: Run AI agents on one Mac and use its windows on another
producthunt.summary_zh: Beam.win是一款软件，可以让你在一台Mac上运行人工智能代理，并在另一台设备上使用这些代理的窗口。它简化了AI工具的跨设备使用，让你更方便地管理和控制多个任务。通过Beam.win，你可以高效地利用AI来完成各类工作。

producthunt.name: Inbox Zero
producthunt.summary_zh: Inbox Zero 是一款开源的电子邮件管理工具，旨在提供高效的邮件处理体验。它类似于 Superhuman，帮助用户快速整理、回复和管理邮件，让收件箱保持整洁。通过简洁的界面和强大的功能，提升工作效率。

producthunt.name: TheySaid 4.0
producthunt.tagline: See how users will react, right where you build.
producthunt.summary_zh: TheySaid 4.0 是一款用户反馈工具，能够让你在产品开发过程中实时查看用户对你设计的反应。用户可以直接在设计界面中留下意见和建议，帮助你更好地优化产品。

github_trending.description: Persistent Context Across Sessions for Every Agent – Captures everything your agent does during sessions, compresses it with AI, and injects relevant context back into future sessions. Works with Claude Code, OpenClaw, Codex, Gemini, Hermes, Copilot, OpenCode + More
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目旨在为人工智能助手提供持久的上下文记忆，使其在多个会话之间能够记住之前的交流内容，从而提升对话的连贯性和相关性。对于Yves来说，这个工具可以帮助Logic Labs在开发更智能的AI应用时提高用户体验，同时也能为TexTale的电商平台提供更加个性化的客户互动，增强品牌与消费者的联系。

github_trending.description: Open-source Grok Bot alternative with a virtual machine that bots can use
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个开源的机器人工具，可以在虚拟环境中运行，帮助开发者创建和管理自动化的聊天机器人。对Yves的Logic Labs（AI公司）特别有帮助，因为它可以作为开发AI聊天助手的基础，提升AI在客户互动和服务中的应用效果。同时，这也能为TexTale提供自动化的客户支持和个性化推荐，优化电商运营。

github_trending.description: The design vocabulary for your coding agent. Steer with polish and bolder, review with critique and audit, catch AI slop before it ships.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目旨在帮助用户通过一种优雅的设计语言，使AI在设计方面表现得更出色。对于Yves来说，这个项目可以帮助Logic Labs提升其AI产品的设计能力，同时也能为TexTale提供更具吸引力的品牌视觉效果，增强电商品牌的市场竞争力。作为创意设计从业者，他可以借助这个工具提高设计效率和质量，更好地实现创意想法。

github_trending.description: Open-source AI coworkers that each get a computer of their own: a browser, files and tools, with every action decided before it happens and recorded after. Bring any AG-UI agent.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个开源的人工智能助手，每个助手都有自己的电脑，能够自主浏览网页、处理文件和使用工具，所有操作都经过预先设定并记录下来。对于Yves来说，这个项目对Logic Labs（AI 公司）有很大的帮助，可以用于开发更智能的AI工具和协作系统，同时也可以激发他的创意设计灵感，提高工作效率。

github_trending.description: 紫微斗数开源排盘引擎 — 基于倪海厦《天纪》体系，含完整排盘算法、四化系统、格局知识库、古籍原文数据
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个用于紫微斗数（中国传统占星术）排盘的开源引擎，它提供了完整的算法和知识库，可以帮助用户快速生成和解析个人命盘。对于Yves来说，这个项目可能对Logic Labs（AI 公司）有帮助，因为他可以探索如何将传统文化和现代AI技术相结合，创造出独特的创意产品。同时，它也激发了他作为创意设计从业者的灵感，寻找将占星元素融入科技服装设计的机会。

github_trending.description: A collection of AI agent skills for working with Expo projects and Expo Application Services
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个集合，提供了多种 AI 代理技能，专门用于处理 Expo 项目和 Expo 应用服务，可以帮助开发者更高效地进行应用开发和管理。对于 Yves 来说，这个项目对 Logic Labs（AI 公司）将特别有帮助，因为它可以帮助他的团队在构建与 AI 相关的应用时，更加快速和高效，提升创意设计过程中的技术实施能力。同时，这也能为 TexTale 的电商平台提供更智能的用户交互体验。

github_trending.description: Macro is a unified workspace for teams: email, chat, docs, tasks, agents, calls, and CRM — @-linked together with shared AI memory.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目Macro是一个为团队提供的多功能工作空间，集成了邮件、聊天、文档、任务、智能助手和客户关系管理等工具，通过共享的AI记忆将这些功能连接在一起，使协作更加高效。对于Yves来说，这个工具可以帮助Logic Labs（AI公司）提升团队的沟通与协作效率，同时也能为TexTale（科技服装电商）提供市场营销和客户关系管理的支持，增强品牌运营能力。作为创意设计从业者，他也可以利用这一平台更好地组织和分享创意。

github_trending.description: Skills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目提供了一套关于真实工程师技能的列表，主要用于帮助开发者更好地管理和组织自己的技能。对于Yves来说，这个项目能够帮助Logic Labs深入了解技术人才的需求，进而优化AI产品的设计和开发，同时也能够为TexTale提供对技术能力的认识，以提升电商平台的科技感和竞争力。
这个项目是一个用 TypeScript 编写的全栈应用开发框架，旨在帮助开发者更快速地构建现代 web 应用。对于 Yves 来说，这个项目可以帮助 TexTale 提高电商平台的开发效率，使其在品牌营销和用户体验上更具竞争力；同时，作为创意设计从业者，他也可以通过这个框架更好地将创意想法转化为实际产品。
DeepTutor 是一个旨在提供个性化终身学习辅导的人工智能系统，可以根据用户的学习进度和需求进行调整，帮助他们更有效地掌握知识。对 Yves 来说，这个项目对于 Logic Labs（AI 公司）尤其有帮助，因为它展示了如何利用 AI 技术提升个性化教育体验，能够激发新的创意和应用场景，同时也能为他在 TexTale 发展创新的销售和市场策略提供灵感。
